title: 03. Databases & Data Modeling: Database Design at Scale
summary: Covers How to Handle Billions of Records Without Slowing Down, SQL vs NoSQL, Database Indexing, Connection Pooling, Read Replicas and more.
objectives: How to Handle Billions of Records Without Slowing Down

sections.title: How to Handle Billions of Records Without Slowing Down

diagrams.title: The usual path for scaling a database
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  a["1 · Indexes + query fixes"] --> b["2 · Connection pooling"]
  b --> c["3 · Cache hot reads"]
  c --> d["4 · Read replicas"]
  d --> e["5 · Vertical scale the primary"]
  e --> f["6 · Partition big tables"]
  f --> g["7 · Shard writes across databases"]
diagrams.explain: Scale the cheapest way first. Most "the database is slow" problems are missing indexes or bad queries; then connection storms (fix with a pooler such as PgBouncer); then repeated reads (cache them). Read replicas and a bigger primary carry you surprisingly far. Partitioning and finally sharding come last because they make every query, migration and transaction harder.

sections.title: 1. SQL vs NoSQL
sections.body:
### When to Use What (Decision Matrix)

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              USE SQL (PostgreSQL/MySQL)                      │
│                                                            │
│  ✅ Data has relationships (users→orders→products)          │
│  ✅ Need ACID transactions (payments, banking)              │
│  ✅ Need complex JOINs and aggregations                     │
│  ✅ Data structure is well-defined and stable                │
│  ✅ Need strong consistency ("read what you wrote")          │
│                                                            │
│  Examples: User accounts, Orders, Payments, Inventory       │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              USE NoSQL (MongoDB/DynamoDB)                    │
│                                                            │
│  ✅ Data is flexible/varies per record                      │
│  ✅ Need horizontal scaling (millions of writes)            │
│  ✅ Need fast reads with simple queries                     │
│  ✅ Data is nested/hierarchical                             │
│  ✅ Schema changes frequently                               │
│                                                            │
│  Examples: Product catalogs, User profiles, Chat messages   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### What Real Companies Use

```
Amazon:
  ├── PostgreSQL/Aurora → Orders, Payments
  ├── DynamoDB → Shopping Cart, Session Data
  ├── Elasticsearch → Product Search
  └── Redis → Caching, Rate Limiting

Instagram:
  ├── PostgreSQL → Users, Followers, Likes
  ├── Cassandra → Feed Data (billions of rows)
  ├── Redis → Caching
  └── Elasticsearch → User/Hashtag Search

ChatGPT:
  ├── PostgreSQL → Users, Subscriptions, API Keys
  ├── Redis → Rate Limiting, Caching
  ├── Vector DB (Pinecone/pgvector) → Embeddings
  └── Object Storage → Conversation History
```

sections.title: 2. Database Indexing
sections.body:
### The Most Important Performance Optimization

```
WITHOUT INDEX (Full Table Scan):
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│ users table (10 million rows)    │
│                                  │
│ SELECT * FROM users              │
│ WHERE email = 'john@example.com' │
│                                  │
│ ↓ Scans ROW BY ROW              │
│ Row 1: alice@... ❌              │
│ Row 2: bob@... ❌                │
│ Row 3: charlie@... ❌            │
│ ...                              │
│ Row 5,847,293: john@... ✅       │
│                                  │
│ Time: 5-10 SECONDS 🐌           │
└──────────────────────────────────┘

WITH INDEX (B-Tree Lookup):
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│ Index on email column            │
│                                  │
│ B-Tree structure:                │
│         [m]                      │
│        /   \                     │
│    [f]      [s]                  │
│    / \      / \                  │
│ [a-e] [g-l] [n-r] [t-z]        │
│              ↓                   │
│         john@... → Row 5847293   │
│                                  │
│ Time: 1-5 MILLISECONDS ⚡       │
└──────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Index Types and When to Use Them

```sql
-- B-Tree (DEFAULT) — Good for =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date ON orders(created_at);

-- Partial Index — Only index rows that match a condition
-- "I only query active users, why index inactive ones?"
CREATE INDEX idx_active_users ON users(email) WHERE is_active = true;

-- Composite Index — Multiple columns
-- Good for: WHERE status = 'active' AND created_at > '2026-01-01'
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_date ON orders(status, created_at);

-- GIN Index — For JSONB, Array, Full-Text Search
CREATE INDEX idx_product_tags ON products USING GIN(tags);

-- Unique Index — Prevents duplicates
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email_unique ON users(email);
```

### Index Strategy for E-commerce

```sql
-- Users table
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);              -- Login
CREATE INDEX idx_users_role ON users(role);                -- Admin queries

-- Products table
CREATE INDEX idx_products_category ON products(category_id); -- Browse
CREATE INDEX idx_products_price ON products(price);          -- Sort by price
CREATE INDEX idx_products_search ON products USING GIN(     -- Full-text search
    to_tsvector('english', name || ' ' || description)
);

-- Orders table
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user ON orders(user_id);            -- "My orders"
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);           -- Admin: pending orders
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date ON orders(created_at DESC);    -- Recent orders

-- ANALYZE what queries are slow:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM products WHERE category_id = 5 AND price < 100;
```

sections.title: 3. Connection Pooling
sections.body:
### Without Connection Pooling (Each Request = New Connection)

```
Request 1 → Open DB Connection → Query → Close Connection
Request 2 → Open DB Connection → Query → Close Connection
Request 3 → Open DB Connection → Query → Close Connection
...
Request 1000 → Open DB Connection → TOO MANY CONNECTIONS! 💀

Opening a connection takes ~50-100ms each time!
PostgreSQL default max_connections = 100
```

### With Connection Pooling

```
App starts → Creates pool of 20 connections ─────────────┐
                                                         │
Request 1 → Borrow connection from pool → Query → Return │
Request 2 → Borrow connection from pool → Query → Return │
Request 3 → Borrow connection from pool → Query → Return │
...                                                      │
Request 1000 → Wait for available connection → Query →   │
                                                         │
Pool maintains 20 connections, reused by thousands of    │
requests. Connection creation overhead = ZERO!           │
```

### FastAPI + SQLAlchemy Connection Pooling

```python
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine, AsyncSession
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker

# Create engine with connection pool
engine = create_async_engine(
    "postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@localhost/mydb",
    pool_size=20,          # Keep 20 connections ready
    max_overflow=10,       # Allow 10 extra during peak
    pool_timeout=30,       # Wait 30s for available connection
    pool_recycle=1800,     # Recycle connections every 30 min
    echo=False,            # Don't log SQL (production)
)

# Session factory
async_session = sessionmaker(engine, class_=AsyncSession, expire_on_commit=False)

# Dependency for FastAPI
async def get_db():
    async with async_session() as session:
        try:
            yield session
            await session.commit()
        except Exception:
            await session.rollback()
            raise
        finally:
            await session.close()

# Usage in routes
@app.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def get_user(user_id: int, db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db)):
    result = await db.execute(select(User).where(User.id == user_id))
    return result.scalar_one_or_none()
```

sections.title: 4. Read Replicas
sections.body:
### The 80/20 Rule: 80% of Database Traffic is READS

```
Problem:
  1 Database server handling ALL traffic:
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │   Primary DB      │ ← 80% reads + 20% writes = OVERLOADED
  └──────────────────┘

Solution: Read Replicas
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │   Primary DB      │ ← Only WRITES (20% of traffic)
  └────────┬─────────┘
           │ Replication (async copy of data)
     ┌─────┼─────┐
     ▼     ▼     ▼
  ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐
  │Replica│ │Replica│ │Replica│ ← All READS go here
  │  1    │ │  2    │ │  3    │   (80% of traffic split 3 ways)
  └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘
```

### Implementation in FastAPI

```python
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine

# Write database (Primary)
write_engine = create_async_engine("postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@primary-db/mydb")

# Read databases (Replicas) — round robin
read_engines = [
    create_async_engine("postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@replica-1/mydb"),
    create_async_engine("postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@replica-2/mydb"),
    create_async_engine("postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@replica-3/mydb"),
]

import itertools
read_engine_cycle = itertools.cycle(read_engines)

async def get_read_db():
    """Get session from a read replica (round robin)"""
    engine = next(read_engine_cycle)
    async with AsyncSession(engine) as session:
        yield session

async def get_write_db():
    """Get session from the primary database"""
    async with AsyncSession(write_engine) as session:
        yield session

# Routes use appropriate database
@app.get("/products")  # READ → Replica
async def list_products(db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_read_db)):
    result = await db.execute(select(Product))
    return result.scalars().all()

@app.post("/products")  # WRITE → Primary
async def create_product(product: ProductCreate, db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_write_db)):
    new_product = Product(**product.dict())
    db.add(new_product)
    await db.commit()
    return new_product
```

sections.title: 5. Database Sharding
sections.body:
### When Even Read Replicas Aren't Enough (Billions of Records)

```
Problem: One database holds ALL users (billions of rows)
  SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 999999999 → SLOW even with index

Solution: Split data across multiple databases (SHARDING)

  Shard Key: user_id

  ┌───────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐
  │   Shard 1     │  │   Shard 2     │  │   Shard 3     │
  │ Users 1-33M   │  │ Users 33M-66M │  │ Users 66M-100M│
  │               │  │               │  │               │
  │ Orders for    │  │ Orders for    │  │ Orders for    │
  │ Users 1-33M   │  │ Users 33M-66M │  │ Users 66M-100M│
  └───────────────┘  └───────────────┘  └───────────────┘

  Each shard = smaller dataset = faster queries!
```

### Sharding Strategies

```
1. Range-Based Sharding:
   Users 1-1M    → Shard A
   Users 1M-2M   → Shard B
   Users 2M-3M   → Shard C
   ❌ Problem: Shard A fills up while C is empty (uneven)

2. Hash-Based Sharding (Most Common):
   shard_number = hash(user_id) % number_of_shards

   hash(user_42) % 3 = 0   → Shard A
   hash(user_43) % 3 = 2   → Shard C
   hash(user_44) % 3 = 1   → Shard B
   ✅ Even distribution!

3. Geography-Based Sharding:
   US users    → US-East database
   EU users    → EU-West database
   Asia users  → AP-Southeast database
   ✅ Lower latency for users!
```

sections.title: 6. Data Modeling for Scale
sections.body:
### E-commerce Database Schema

```sql
-- ═══ POSTGRESQL SCHEMA FOR SCALABLE E-COMMERCE ═══

-- Users (PostgreSQL — relational, needs ACID for auth)
CREATE TABLE users (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    role VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'buyer',
    is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT true,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Products (could also be MongoDB — flexible schema)
CREATE TABLE products (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    seller_id BIGINT REFERENCES users(id),
    name VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,
    description TEXT,
    price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    category_id INTEGER,
    stock INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    metadata JSONB,  -- Flexible: color, size, weight, etc.
    search_vector TSVECTOR,  -- Full-text search
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Orders (PostgreSQL — ACID is critical for orders!)
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id BIGINT REFERENCES users(id),
    status VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'pending',
    total_amount DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
    shipping_address JSONB NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id BIGINT REFERENCES orders(id),
    product_id BIGINT REFERENCES products(id),
    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL,
    price_at_purchase DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL
);

-- Reviews
CREATE TABLE reviews (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id BIGINT REFERENCES users(id),
    product_id BIGINT REFERENCES products(id),
    rating SMALLINT CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
    comment TEXT,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    UNIQUE(user_id, product_id)  -- One review per user per product
);
```

sections.title: 7. MongoDB at Scale
sections.body:
### Aggregation Pipeline for Analytics

```python
from motor.motor_asyncio import AsyncIOMotorClient

client = AsyncIOMotorClient("mongodb://localhost:27017")
db = client.ecommerce

# Example: Top selling products this month
pipeline = [
    {"$match": {
        "created_at": {"$gte": datetime(2026, 1, 1)},
        "status": "completed"
    }},
    {"$unwind": "$items"},
    {"$group": {
        "_id": "$items.product_id",
        "total_sold": {"$sum": "$items.quantity"},
        "revenue": {"$sum": {"$multiply": ["$items.price", "$items.quantity"]}}
    }},
    {"$sort": {"revenue": -1}},
    {"$limit": 10}
]

top_products = await db.orders.aggregate(pipeline).to_list(length=10)
```

### MongoDB Indexes for Performance

```python
# Create indexes for common queries
await db.users.create_index("email", unique=True)
await db.users.create_index("username", unique=True)

await db.products.create_index([("category", 1), ("price", 1)])
await db.products.create_index({"name": "text", "description": "text"})  # Full-text

await db.orders.create_index([("user_id", 1), ("created_at", -1)])
await db.orders.create_index("status")

# Compound index for feed queries
await db.posts.create_index([("user_id", 1), ("created_at", -1)])
```

sections.title: 8. PostgreSQL at Scale
sections.body:
### Performance Tuning

```sql
-- Check slow queries
SELECT query, calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- Check index usage (are your indexes being used?)
SELECT schemaname, tablename, indexname, idx_scan, idx_tup_read
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
ORDER BY idx_scan ASC;  -- Low scan count = unused index

-- Table sizes
SELECT tablename,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(tablename::regclass))
FROM pg_tables WHERE schemaname = 'public'
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(tablename::regclass) DESC;
```

### PostgreSQL Configuration for High Traffic

```ini
# postgresql.conf optimizations for 1M+ users

# Memory
shared_buffers = 4GB              # 25% of total RAM
effective_cache_size = 12GB       # 75% of total RAM
work_mem = 64MB                   # Per-query sort memory

# Connections
max_connections = 200             # Use connection pooler (PgBouncer)

# Write Performance
wal_buffers = 64MB
checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9
max_wal_size = 4GB

# Query Planner
random_page_cost = 1.1            # If using SSD
effective_io_concurrency = 200    # If using SSD
```

sections.title: 9. Database Patterns in Real Apps
sections.body:
### Pattern: Soft Deletes

```sql
-- Don't actually delete data (for audit trail, recovery)
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL;

-- "Delete" a user
UPDATE users SET deleted_at = NOW() WHERE id = 42;

-- Query only active users
SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- Partial index for performance (only index active records)
CREATE INDEX idx_active_users ON users(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
```

### Pattern: Optimistic Locking (Prevent Race Conditions)

```python
# Problem: Two users buy the LAST item simultaneously
# User A reads stock=1, User B reads stock=1
# Both proceed to buy → stock goes to -1!

# Solution: Version-based optimistic locking
@app.post("/orders")
async def create_order(order: OrderCreate, db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db)):
    # 1. Read product with current version
    product = await db.get(Product, order.product_id)

    if product.stock < order.quantity:
        raise HTTPException(400, "Out of stock")

    # 2. Try to update with version check
    result = await db.execute(
        update(Product)
        .where(Product.id == order.product_id)
        .where(Product.version == product.version)  # Only if version matches!
        .values(
            stock=Product.stock - order.quantity,
            version=Product.version + 1
        )
    )

    if result.rowcount == 0:
        # Someone else modified it! Retry.
        raise HTTPException(409, "Conflict — please retry")

    # 3. Create order
    new_order = Order(**order.dict())
    db.add(new_order)
    await db.commit()
    return new_order
```

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.body:
```
1. INDEX everything you query frequently
2. Use CONNECTION POOLING (never open/close per request)
3. READ REPLICAS for read-heavy workloads (80/20 rule)
4. SHARDING for billions of records
5. SQL for transactions, NoSQL for flexibility
6. EXPLAIN ANALYZE your slow queries
7. Use JSONB in PostgreSQL for flexible fields
8. SOFT DELETES for audit trails
9. OPTIMISTIC LOCKING for concurrent updates
```
